# Acme's point of view
_18 Nov 2026 · 2 stances · 4 pages read · 2 questions for the founders_

> **Our worldview.** Agents are worth having when a team can trust them with real work, and that trust is earned. We start agents under review and widen what they may do as the record grows, and we judge them on day thirty, not in the demo.

## At a glance

| # | Stance | Pillar | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Autonomy is earned, not switched on** | Governance | 🟢 Strong |
| 2 | **The test is day thirty, not the demo** | Production | 🟢 Strong |

## Questions for the founders

1. **Agent pricing:** Our writing does not say how agents should be priced: per run, per seat or per outcome. Which is it?
2. **Approval queue:** The platform page still says "approval queue"; the 10 Nov update retired it in favour of the change log. Which is current?

---

## 1. Autonomy is earned, not switched on

**Governance** · 🟢 Strong · 2 sources · Angles: Contrarian · Lesson from building

> **Our stance.** Agents earn the right to act on their own by running under review first. Control comes before autonomy, not after.

The usual approach is to decide up front how much an agent may do, then add checks when something breaks. We do it the other way round. Every change an agent makes is reviewed before it reaches production, and that record of reviewed runs is what tells a team it can trust the agent with more.

| Most people believe | We believe |
|---|---|
| Give the agent full autonomy now and add guardrails when problems show up. | Start under review, and widen what the agent may do as its record of reviewed runs grows. |

### Why we believe it

1. **Autonomy comes from a track record**
   > “Autonomy is something an agent earns after it has run under review, not a setting you switch on.” [Approvals before autonomy](https://acme.example.com/blog/approvals-before-autonomy)
2. **Review happens before production**
   > “Every agent change goes through review before it reaches production.” [Platform](https://acme.example.com/platform)

### Proof

- **Reviewers see each change before it lands.** “Reviewers see a short summary of each change in the change log and confirm it before it runs.” [Approvals before autonomy](https://acme.example.com/blog/approvals-before-autonomy)

### Where we concede

Our writing does not say where this stops applying.

### Why a buyer should care

An operations lead gets an agent they can expand step by step, with the reviewed runs to show why each step was safe.

### Use it when

- A vendor announces fully autonomous agents.
- A company reports an agent that changed something nobody reviewed.

### Our words

| Say | Never say |
|---|---|
| "not a setting you switch on" | "approval queue" (retired 10 Nov; reviews now happen in the change log) |
|  | That a person must approve every action forever. |

### Open questions

- [ ] Where does this stop applying? For example, read-only agents.

---

## 2. The test is day thirty, not the demo

**Production** · 🟢 Strong · 2 sources · Angles: Myth vs reality · Prediction

> **Our stance.** Most agent demos never reach production. An agent proves itself by still working on day thirty, and that takes an owner.

A demo shows that an agent can work once. Teams keep the agents that still work weeks later, and those are the ones a person owns after launch. We keep seeing the same pattern with customers: most demos never survive their first week in a real team.

| Most people believe | We believe |
|---|---|
| A strong demo shows the agent is ready. | A demo is a promise. Only an owner and a month of real runs show the agent is ready. |

### Why we believe it

1. **Working once is not the bar**
   > “A demo that works once is not an agent; an agent is the thing that still works on day thirty.” [Why demos die](https://acme.example.com/blog/why-demos-die)
2. **We see demos die in real teams**
   > “most agent demos never survive their first week in a real team.” (founder notes)
3. **The agents that last have an owner**
   > “The ones that last have a person who owns them after launch.” (founder notes)

### Where we concede

Our writing does not say where this stops applying.

### Why a buyer should care

A buyer comparing agent vendors should ask what happens in week four, not what happens in the demo.

### Use it when

- A company shows an agent demo or benchmark with no production use.
- A survey reports agent projects being abandoned.

### Our words

| Say | Never say |
|---|---|
| "still works on day thirty" | A failure rate we have not measured. |

### Open questions

- [ ] Where does this stop applying?
- [ ] Can we name a customer whose agent made it past day thirty?

---

## How this was made

- **Read:** 4 pages on acme.example.com, plus founder notes.
- **Updates respected:** "approval queue" → reviews in the change log (10 Nov update)
- **Left out:** 4 candidate stances (1 not on our domains, 2 took no side, 1 generic).
- Every quote is copied word for word from the linked page. Approve or correct the stances, then pass corrections back as `feedback` on the next run.
